newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIAN POWER SUPPLIES NOT YET HIT BY STRIKE.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIAN POWER SUPPLIES NOT YET HIT BY STRIKE.

text.p: Bulgaria's power supplies are showing no immediate effects from a general strike organised by opposition supporters, government officials said on Monday.
"We have no reasons to expect any problems with power supplies over the next three weeks," National Electricity Company spokesman Srebri Valchev told Reuters.

The biggest mines which supply the Bulgaria's major thermal plants with coal were on strike on Monday. They included the Maritsa East, Bobov Dol, Marbas, Pernik and Bistritsa mining regions, said Energy Ministry spokeswoman Radost Pateva.
The Maritsa East mines, which supply 30 percent of Bulgaria's power needs, have coal supplies to last for three weeks, said Valchev.
The mines held one-hour stoppages last week. Half of them went on full strike on Sunday and the rest joined on Monday.
The strikers said they were determined to hold out for as long as necessary.
"We will resume work only when the Socialists step down from power and refuse to form a second government," said Ivan Dimitrov of the Maritsa East strike committee.
The Kozloduy nuclear power plant, which produces around 40 percent of the country's needs, is operating at 82.4 percent of capacity and covers the country's electricity needs so far, said Valchev.

Protestors at Bulgaria's biggest oil refinery Neftohim, near the Black Sea port of Bourgas, have staged one-hour work stoppages of the oil product shipments section since Thursday but the refinery's worst problem is crude supply.

The Bourgas-based refinery processes 13,500 tonnes per day since Friday, down from average output for last year of around 18,000 tonnes, said Neftohim spokeswoman Tania Hadjieva. Oil supplies amounted to 49,000 tonnes and 70,000 tonne oil tanker was expected to arrive on Tuesday, she said.
Some petrol pump stations around the country reported fuel shortages. Local media said that Neftochim's output has fallen to 8,000 tonnes a day.
Russia's Rosneft said on Tuesday it had reduced crude supplies to Neftohim because of unpaid debts and political uncertainty.
Bulgaria's government has been paralysed since December when Socialist prime minister Zhan Videnov resigned after months of criticism of his handling of the economy.
The opposition, which wants immediate elections, stepped up protests last week after the Socialists accepted a mandate to form a new cabinet. - Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-84561
